claim: Undershooting targets is the optimal strategy given that uncertainty over position scales supra-linearly with time and distance travelled
source: Undershooting targets is, in fact, the optimal strategy given that the uncertainty over one's own and the firefly's position scales supra-linearly with time and distance travelled (see Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018).
evidence: Reference to prior work by Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018

claim: The target-tracking index averaged 0.73 (95% CI = [0.72, 0.74]) during the first second of each trial across all animals and sessions
source: Across all animals and sessions, the target-tracking index averaged 0.73 (95% CI = [0.72, 0.74]) during the first second of each trial.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of eye tracking behavior across all experimental sessions

claim: Monkeys attempted to maintain their gaze on the target even after it had disappeared
source: This suggest that, while not a task requirement, animals developed the strategy of fixating on the visible firefly and then attempted to maintain their gaze on it even after the target had disappeared (Figure 1G, see Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2020, for a full description of this phenomenon and demonstration that pursuing the invisible firefly with our eyes results in improved task performance).
evidence: Behavioral observation supported by reference to prior work

claim: 231 units were recorded from MSTd across 82 sessions
source: We recorded single-unit activity from a large number of neurons in MSTd (231 units), area 7a (3200 units), and dlPFC (823 units) across 82 sessions while monkeys performed the firefly task (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: 3200 units were recorded from area 7a across 82 sessions
source: We recorded single-unit activity from a large number of neurons in MSTd (231 units), area 7a (3200 units), and dlPFC (823 units) across 82 sessions while monkeys performed the firefly task (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: 823 units were recorded from dlPFC across 82 sessions
source: We recorded single-unit activity from a large number of neurons in MSTd (231 units), area 7a (3200 units), and dlPFC (823 units) across 82 sessions while monkeys performed the firefly task (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The average cross-validated pseudo-R² of the P-GAM model was 0.072
source: The average cross-validated pseudo-R2 was 0.072 (see Colin Cameron and Windmeijer, 1997).
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit quality

claim: The P-GAM included 17 analog or digital task inputs
source: In total, the encoding model had 17 (analog or digital) task inputs (Figure 2C), in addition to hundreds of potential lateral and across region coupling filters

claim: MSTd showed the highest proportion of neurons coding for eye position with 58.8% for vertical and 63.3% for horizontal eye position
source: Namely, the fraction of neurons tuned to sensorimotor variables was highest in area 7a (linear and angular velocity, linear and angular acceleration, time of movement onset and offset, all p<0.01; Cohen's d linear acceleration d=0.2, all the rest d>0.76), while most neurons in MSTd coded for eye position (58.8% and 63.3% respectively for vertical and horizontal eye position).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neural tuning properties

claim: Area 7a showed the highest fraction of neurons tuned to sensorimotor variables
source: Namely, the fraction of neurons tuned to sensorimotor variables was highest in area 7a (linear and angular velocity, linear and angular acceleration, time of movement onset and offset, all p<0.01; Cohen's d linear acceleration d=0.2, all the rest d>0.76)

claim: Neurons in area 7a showed a strong dependency to the phase of ongoing LFP fluctuations
source: Neurons in area 7a showed a strong dependency to the phase of ongoing LFP fluctuations (see Figure 2—figure supplement 8 for further illustrations of this effect as quantified by the P-GAM, and Figure 2—figure supplement 9 for corroborative evidence by pairwise phase consistency, Vinck et al., 2010), a fact that was less observed in dlPFC or MSTd (all p<7.1 × 10–8, all d>1.02).
evidence: Statistical analysis with supporting figures and citation to validation method

claim: The greatest fraction of neurons encoding for path integration and spatial goals were in dlPFC, ranging from 30.6% to 57.5%
source: Lastly, and most relevant to the task of path integrating to the location of invisible fireflies, we observed that the greatest fraction of neurons encoding for both path integration (i.e., travelled distance and angle turned) and the distance and angle to the target (i.e., spatial goal) were in dlPFC (ranging from 30.6% to 57.5%).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of neural encoding properties

claim: Area 7a had more neurons coding for path integration than MSTd (all p<1.6 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.54)
source: Interestingly, while 7a had more neurons coding for path integration than MSTd (all p<1.6 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.54), the latter area had a greater fraction of neurons coding for the latent distance and angle to target than 7a did (all p<6.1 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.41).

claim: MSTd had a greater fraction of neurons coding for the latent distance and angle to target than area 7a (all p<6.1 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.41)
source: Interestingly, while 7a had more neurons coding for path integration than MSTd (all p<1.6 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.54), the latter area had a greater fraction of neurons coding for the latent distance and angle to target than 7a did (all p<6.1 × 10–5, all Cohen's d>0.41).

claim: The distributions of preferred distances/angles from origin and to target spanned the entire range of angles and distances visited, demonstrating a full basis set covering the feature space
source: The distributions shown in Figure 3B illustrate that the preferred distances/angles from origin and to target spanned the entire range of angles and distances visited, demonstrating a full basis set covering the feature space.
evidence: Visual and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Angles specifying a 0° offset from the heading at origin were over-represented across all animals
source: Across all animals, angles specifying a 0° offset from the heading at origin were over-represented (Figure 3C, top row, proportions across all animals), while the 0° offset from target location was under-represented (Figure 3C, second row).

claim: The 0° offset from target location was under-represented
source: Across all animals, angles specifying a 0° offset from the heading at origin were over-represented (Figure 3C, top row, proportions across all animals), while the 0° offset from target location was under-represented (Figure 3C, second row).

claim: The distribution of preferred angles to target was bimodal in area 7a and dlPFC (bimodality coefficients: 7a=0.89, dlPFC=0.80, both p<0.05)
source: Instead, particularly in area 7a and dlPFC, the distribution of preferred angles to target was bimodal (bimodality coefficients, null = 0.55, MST = 0.57, 7a=0.89, dlPFC = 0.80, 7a and dlPFC p<0.05), with many neurons showing a preference for ~45–90° away from target, either leftward or rightward.

claim: Many neurons in area 7a and dlPFC showed a preference for ~45–90° away from target, either leftward or rightward
source: Instead, particularly in area 7a and dlPFC, the distribution of preferred angles to target was bimodal (bimodality coefficients, null = 0.55, MST = 0.57, 7a=0.89, dlPFC = 0.80, 7a and dlPFC p<0.05), with many neurons showing a preference for ~45–90° away from target, either leftward or rightward.

claim: The reversed pattern of preferences between cortex and hippocampus may suggest that cortex plays a role in guiding heading toward the desired state while hippocampus maintains this heading
source: Speculatively, this reversed pattern of preferences between cortex (here) and hippocampus (Sarel et al., 2017) may suggest that while the former plays a role in guiding heading toward the desired state (akin to an error or correction signal), the hippocampus maintains this heading.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on comparison with prior work

claim: MSTd, area 7a, and dlPFC all showed an over-representation of units coding for distances near to the starting location (<~150 cm)
source: In terms of radial distance, MSTd, area 7a, and dlPFC all showed an over-representation of units coding for distances near to, as opposed to far from, the starting location (Figure 3C, third row, <~150 cm).

claim: Area 7a showed a strong preference for nearby targets with approximately 50% of units coding for targets within ~30 cm
source: Area 7a showed a strong preference for nearby targets with approximately 50% of units coding for targets within ~30 cm.

claim: Neurons in MSTd and dlPFC responded primarily at intermediary and far distances from the target (~200–400 cm from target)
source: Neurons in MSTd and dlPFC, on the other hand, responded primarily at intermediary and far distances from the target (~200–400 cm from target; Figure 3C, fourth row).
evidence: Analysis of distance tuning preferences shown in Figure 3C

claim: Nearly all MSTd (89%) and dlPFC (94%) neurons were categorized as belonging within the same cluster defined by true mixed selectivity
source: This approach (see Methods for details) showed that nearly all MSTd (89%) and dlPFC (94%) neurons were categorized as belonging within the same cluster (Figure 4A, cluster number 1), one that was defined by true mixed selectivity (Figure 4B, top left).
evidence: Statistical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Area 7a neurons appeared in three distinct clusters (36%, 22%, and 31%)
source: In contrast, area 7a neurons appeared in three distinct clusters (Figure 4A, cluster numbers 1–3, respectively, 36%, 22%, and 31%).
evidence: Statistical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: 37% of neurons in dlPFC were tuned to the ongoing LFP phase within the beta range in area 7a
source: Most notably, 37% of neurons in dlPFC were tuned to the ongoing LFP phase within the beta range in area 7a.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of inter-area LFP-spike coupling

claim: 59% of neurons in area 7a were modulated by the ongoing phase of beta-band LFP in dlPFC
source: An even greater proportion of units showed the reciprocal property, with 59% of neurons in area 7a being modulated by the ongoing phase of beta-band LFP in dlPFC.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of inter-area LFP-spike coupling

claim: 24% of area 7a units were modulated by the ongoing phase of alpha-band LFP in MSTd
source: A considerable proportion of 7a units were also modulated by the ongoing phase of alpha-band LFP in MSTd (24%, Figure 4D).

claim: There were more units coupled in MSTd (13%) and area 7a (22%) than in dlPFC (7%)
source: There were more units coupled in MSTd (13%, corrected for distance between electrodes, see Methods) and area 7a (22%) than in dlPFC (7%, Figure 4E)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of unit-to-unit coupling shown in Figure 4E

claim: 12% of neurons in dlPFC were coupled to activity in MSTd
source: Twelve percent of neurons in dlPFC were coupled to activity in MSTd, while 7% of neurons in MSTd were coupled to activity in dlPFC.

claim: 7% of neurons in MSTd were coupled to activity in dlPFC
source: Twelve percent of neurons in dlPFC were coupled to activity in MSTd, while 7% of neurons in MSTd were coupled to activity in dlPFC.

claim: Neither MSTd nor dlPFC showed a feedforward or feedback likelihood of being coupled with area 7a that exceeded 4%
source: Importantly, neither of these regions showed either a 'feedforward' or 'feedback' likelihood of being coupled with area 7a that exceeded 4% (Figure 4E).

claim: The more similar the tuning functions were between two neurons, the more likely these were to be coupled
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 3D shows that the more similar the tuning functions were between two neurons, the more likely these were to be coupled.

claim: The mean absolute difference between a monkey's eye position and where they ought to be looking if perfectly tracking the firefly correlated with steering endpoint error (r²=0.36±0.22)
source: Indeed, within a session and across trials, the mean absolute difference between a monkey's eye position and where they ought to be looking if they were perfectly tracking the firefly correlated with steering endpoint error (r2 ± standard deviation across all datasets, 0.36±0.22; for shuffled data, 0.16±0.09, p=5.6 × 10–3, paired t-test; see Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2020, for the original description of this effect).
evidence: Statistical analysis with comparison to shuffled control and citation to prior work

claim: Better target tracking correlated with less angular bias (r²=0.43, p=0.004)
source: Further, this relationship also held across sessions, with better target tracking correlating with less bias (slopes closer to 1, see Figure 1C), particularly in the angular domain (r2=0.43, p=0.004; radial: r2=0.26, p=0.04; Figure 5A)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Better target tracking correlated with less radial bias (r²=0.26, p=0.04)
source: Further, this relationship also held across sessions, with better target tracking correlating with less bias (slopes closer to 1, see Figure 1C), particularly in the angular domain (r2=0.43, p=0.004; radial: r2=0.26, p=0.04; Figure 5A)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Better target tracking correlated with an increasing proportion of rewarded trials (r²=0.24, p=0.042)
source: Further, this relationship also held across sessions, with better target tracking correlating with less bias (slopes closer to 1, see Figure 1C), particularly in the angular domain (r2=0.43, p=0.004; radial: r2=0.26, p=0.04; Figure 5A), and with an increasing proportion of rewarded trials (r2=0.24, p=0.042).

claim: There was a strong association between the fraction of units showing MST-to-dlPFC coupling and the monkeys' ability to track the hidden firefly with their eyes (r²=0.63, p=0.003)
source: As shown in Figure 5B (top right), we observed a strong association between the fraction of units showing MST-to-dlPFC coupling and the monkeys' ability to track the hidden firefly with their eyes (r2=0.63, p=0.003).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The association between coupling and target tracking was also true for the feedback projection from dlPFC-to-MSTd (r²=0.41, p=0.035)
source: This association, with more coupling indexing better tracking of the firefly, was also true for the 'feedback' projection from dlPFC-to-MSTd (r2=0.41, p=0.035, Figure 5B, bottom left)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The association between coupling and target tracking was also true for dlPFC-to-dlPFC coupling (r²=0.43, p=0.047)
source: This association, with more coupling indexing better tracking of the firefly, was also true for the 'feedback' projection from dlPFC-to-MSTd (r2=0.41, p=0.035, Figure 5B, bottom left), as well as for dlPFC-to-dlPFC coupling (r2=0.43, p=0.047, Figure 5B, bottom right).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: There was no correlation between unit-to-unit couplings within a session and either radial or angular biases (7a-7a coupling vs. angular bias p=0.06; all other p>0.12)
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, there was no correlation between the unit-to-unit couplings within a session, and either radial or angular biases (7a-7a coupling vs. angular bias p=0.06; all other p>0.12).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: There was no correlation between the proportion of rewarded trials in a session and unit-to-unit coupling probability (all p>0.11, Bonferroni corrected)
source: There was similarly no correlation between the proportion of rewarded trials in a session and unit-to-unit coupling probability (all p>0.11, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Statistical analysis with multiple comparison correction

claim: Severing the loop between action and perception disrupts the natural timing that exists between sensory events and internal neural dynamics
source: First, severing the loop between action and perception disrupts the natural timing that exists between sensory events and internal neural dynamics.

claim: Neural excitability in primary visual cortex is enhanced at saccade offset
source: Indeed, work from active sensing, for example, Schroeder et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2016, has shown that neural excitability in primary visual cortex (Barczak et al., 2019) and the anterior nuclei of the thalamus (Leszczynski et al., 2020) are enhanced at saccade offset – precisely when new observations are made.

claim: Neural excitability in the anterior nuclei of the thalamus is enhanced at saccade offset
source: Indeed, work from active sensing, for example, Schroeder et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2016, has shown that neural excitability in primary visual cortex (Barczak et al., 2019) and the anterior nuclei of the thalamus (Leszczynski et al., 2020) are enhanced at saccade offset – precisely when new observations are made.

claim: Enhancement of neural excitability at saccade offset is likely mediated by phase-reset of neural oscillations caused by shifting gaze
source: This enhancement is likely mediated by phase-reset of neural oscillations (Lakatos et al., 2008; Rajkai et al., 2008) caused by the shifting gaze.
evidence: Inference based on cited prior work

claim: Redundancy has been observed between parietal and frontal cortices during visual feature categorization
source: For instance, notorious redundancy has been observed between parietal and frontal cortices with both areas showing similar properties during visual feature categorization (Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012), target selection (Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013), visuo-spatial memory (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 1998), and working memory (Olesen et al., 2004), among others (see Katsuki and Constantinidis, 2012, for a review).

claim: Redundancy between parietal and frontal cortices is an adaptive feature
source: While this redundancy is certainly an adaptive feature (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014; Driscoll et al., 2017), the joint characterization of sensory, parietal, and frontal areas during tasks requiring a flow of cognitive operations typical of daily life (e.g., sensing, memorizing, acting) may offer the possibility to study how these regions differ, and how they interact.

claim: MSTd, area 7a, and dlPFC form a series of reciprocally interconnected areas
source: We record from these regions (MSTd, 7a, and dlPFC) because they form a series of reciprocally interconnected areas (Andersen et al., 1990; Rozzi et al., 2006) that are well established in the processing of optic flow for self-motion, sensorimotor transformations, and belief formation/working memory, all critical elements of the task

claim: MSTd, area 7a, and dlPFC are well established in the processing of optic flow for self-motion, sensorimotor transformations, and belief formation/working memory
source: We record from these regions (MSTd, 7a, and dlPFC) because they form a series of reciprocally interconnected areas (Andersen et al., 1990; Rozzi et al., 2006) that are well established in the processing of optic flow for self-motion, sensorimotor transformations, and belief formation/working memory, all critical elements of the task (see, e.g., Kravitz et al., 2011; Constantinidis and Klingberg, 2016; Christophel et al., 2017; Noel and Angelaki, 2022, for reviews).

claim: All areas probed encode latent task variables
source: We observe that all areas probed – including MSTd, a classically considered sensory area – encode latent task variables.
evidence: Summary of main findings from the study

claim: Global encoding profiles and unit-to-unit couplings suggested a functional subnetwork composed by dlPFC and MSTd
source: Further, global encoding profiles and unit-to-unit couplings suggested a functional subnetwork composed by dlPFC and MSTd (and not area 7a, as would be predicted from anatomy).
evidence: Summary of main findings from the study

claim: The MSTd-dlPFC subnetwork reflects the natural task strategy wherein monkeys continuously gaze toward the location of the invisible target
source: We suggest this MSTd-dlPFC subnetwork reflects the natural task strategy wherein monkeys continuously gaze toward the location of the (invisible) target.

claim: Targets were displayed for 300 ms on a ground plane composed of triangular optic flow elements
source: Targets ('fireflies') were displayed for 300 ms on a ground plane composed of triangular optic flow elements that appeared transiently (250 ms) with random orientations.

claim: The density of optic flow elements was 5 elements/m²
source: The density of these optic flow elements was 5 elements/m2.

claim: Firefly targets were uniformly distributed within a radial range of 1–4 m and an angular eccentricity spanning from –40° to 40° of visual angle
source: The firefly targets were uniformly distributed (across trials) within a radial range of 1–4 m, and an angular eccentricity spanning from –40° (leftward) to 40° (rightward) of visual angle (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Description of experimental design shown in Figure 1

claim: The P-GAM never excluded the distance to target from its selected model when this variable had not been zeroed (0.0% false negative)
source: Across all simulation (n=1344), the P-GAM never excluded the distance to target from its selected model when this variable had not been zeroed (0.0% false negative), and only once failed to exclude this variable from its final selection when the variable had been zeroed (0.0007% false positive).

claim: The P-GAM had a false positive rate of 0.0007% in excluding zeroed variables
source: Across all simulation (n=1344), the P-GAM never excluded the distance to target from its selected model when this variable had not been zeroed (0.0% false negative), and only once failed to exclude this variable from its final selection when the variable had been zeroed (0.0007% false positive).

claim: The reduced model had on average 18.9% the number of parameters as in the full model
source: While the reduced model has on average 18.9% the number of parameters as in the full model (B) its ability to account for neural activity is comparable to the full model.
evidence: Comparison of model complexity shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The reduced model's ability to account for neural activity is comparable to the full model despite having fewer parameters
source: While the reduced model has on average 18.9% the number of parameters as in the full model (B) its ability to account for neural activity is comparable to the full model.
evidence: Model comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Virtual and real-world navigation may rely on partially distinct neural codes
source: For instance, virtual and real-world navigation may rely on partially distinct neural codes (Aghajan et al., 2015).

claim: Eye movements in the current experiment may partially reflect intended head movements
source: This would also allow for independent eye and head movements (head was restrained here) and thus we could estimate whether eye movements in the current experiment partially reflected intended head movements (as they seemingly do in rodents; Michaiel et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation based on cited rodent studies

claim: The anterior hippocampus and prefrontal cortex may abstractly plan goal-directed trajectories
source: Together with the current findings, and the fact that anterior and posterior hippocampus respectively project to the prefrontal and parietal cortex (Strange et al., 2014) suggests that a circuit including the anterior hippocampus and prefrontal cortex may abstractly plan goal-directed trajectories, while a circuit including the posterior hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex may compute body-centric sensorimotor affordances.
evidence: Inference based on current findings and cited anatomical work

claim: A circuit including the posterior hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex may compute body-centric sensorimotor affordances
source: Together with the current findings, and the fact that anterior and posterior hippocampus respectively project to the prefrontal and parietal cortex (Strange et al., 2014) suggests that a circuit including the anterior hippocampus and prefrontal cortex may abstractly plan goal-directed trajectories, while a circuit including the posterior hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex may compute body-centric sensorimotor affordances.
evidence: Inference based on current findings and cited anatomical work

claim: Early on observers may compute their ongoing distance from the origin, and then switch to computing distance from the target
source: The fact that all areas probed showed a preference for distances near (as opposed to far) from where the monkey started path integrating (i.e., the origin) may suggest a change in the computations undertaken early vs. late within a single trajectory. Namely, early on observers may compute their ongoing distance from the origin, and then switch to computing distance not from origin, but from the target.

claim: A switch from first coding displacement from origin to then coding location relative to a target has been previously suggested empirically and in computational accounts
source: This switch from first coding displacement from origin to then coding location relative to a target has been previously suggested empirically (Gothard et al., 1996) and in recent computational accounts (Kanitscheider and Fiete, 2017).
evidence: Citations to prior empirical and computational work

claim: Navigating to a remembered target may involve two interdependent but separable computations: estimating own location relative to a starting location and estimating the position of the target
source: The third major finding relates to the functional organization across MSTd, area 7a, and dlPFC, and again suggests that navigating to a remembered target may involve two interdependent but separable computations: (i) estimating own's own location relative to a starting location (i.e., a landmark) and (ii) estimating the position of the target and discounting self-location from target location.

claim: Anatomical tracer studies suggest a distributed hierarchy with recurrent connections between MSTd and 7a, and between 7a and dlPFC
source: Indeed, anatomical tracer studies suggest a distributed hierarchy, with recurrent connections between MSTd and 7a, and then recurrent connections between 7a and dlPFC (Andersen et al., 1990; Rozzi et al., 2006).

claim: The MSTd-7a-dlPFC pathway may be primarily involved in path integration as opposed to the vector coding of spatial goals
source: In other words, we observed that the coarse channels of communication riding on LFPs are in line with anatomy. Further, the strong tuning of area 7a to sensorimotor variables and the strong tuning of both area 7a and dlPFC (but not MSTd) to the distance and angle from origin suggest that this pathway may be primarily involved in path integration as opposed to the vector coding of spatial goals.
evidence: Inference based on observed tuning properties

claim: Despite the lack of direct anatomical connections, MSTd and dlPFC may form a functional subnetwork within this closed-loop navigate-to-target task
source: These results suggest that despite the lack of direct anatomical connections, MSTd and dlPFC may form a functional subnetwork within this closed-loop navigate-to-target task.

claim: The dynamic functional coupling between MSTd and dlPFC may reflect the innate task strategy monkeys adapted in pursuing the goal location with their eyes
source: Thus, we suggest that the dynamic functional coupling between MSTd and dlPFC may reflect the innate task strategy monkeys adapted in pursuing the goal location with their eyes.

claim: The functional connection between MSTd and dlPFC must be subserved by structure such as a third area not recorded from
source: We report a functional subnetwork between MSTd and dlPFC based on the similarity of their encoding profiles (though they are of course not identical) and the likelihood of encountering unit-to-unit couplings across these areas. But this functional connection must be subserved by structure (e.g., perhaps a third area we did not record from fluctuating with both MSTd and dlPFC).

claim: Mixed yet patterned single cell selectivity is a broad principle of neural computation during closed action-perception loops
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate what may be broad principles of neural computation during closed action-perception loops: (i) mixed yet patterned single cell selectivity, (ii) coding of latent variables even in areas traditionally considered as purely sensory, and (iii) differential coarse (e.g., LFP-spike phase alignment) and fine-grain connectivity between task-relevant areas.

claim: Coding of latent variables occurs even in areas traditionally considered as purely sensory
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate what may be broad principles of neural computation during closed action-perception loops: (i) mixed yet patterned single cell selectivity, (ii) coding of latent variables even in areas traditionally considered as purely sensory, and (iii) differential coarse (e.g., LFP-spike phase alignment) and fine-grain connectivity between task-relevant areas.

claim: Differential coarse and fine-grain connectivity between task-relevant areas is a broad principle of neural computation during closed action-perception loops
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate what may be broad principles of neural computation during closed action-perception loops: (i) mixed yet patterned single cell selectivity, (ii) coding of latent variables even in areas traditionally considered as purely sensory, and (iii) differential coarse (e.g., LFP-spike phase alignment) and fine-grain connectivity between task-relevant areas.

claim: Coupling between sensory and prefrontal areas may reflect embodied task strategies
source: Most notoriously, here we indexed the presence of significant noise correlations between MSTd and dlPFC, independently from 7a. We suggest that this coupling between sensory and prefrontal areas may reflect (embodied) task strategies.

claim: All surgeries and procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Baylor College of Medicine (Protocol A3317-01) and New York University (Protocol number 18-1502)
source: All surgeries and procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Baylor College of Medicine (Protocol A3317-01) and New York University (Protocol number 18-1502) and were in accordance with National Institutes of Health guidelines.

claim: The maximum linear speed was fixed to 2 m/s
source: The maximum linear and angular speeds were fixed to 2 m/s and 90 deg/s.

claim: The maximum angular speed was fixed to 90 deg/s
source: The maximum linear and angular speeds were fixed to 2 m/s and 90 deg/s.

claim: The virtual camera was positioned at a height of 0.1 m above the ground plane
source: The virtual camera was positioned at a height of 0.1 m above the ground plane.

claim: Depth cues included linear perspective, texture gradient, and motion parallax
source: Given the OpenGL approach in re-positioning a virtual camera within a 3D space, depth cues included linear perspective, texture gradient, and motion parallax.

claim: The stimulus was rendered as a red-green anaglyph to provide binocular parallax
source: Further, the stimulus was rendered as a red-green anaglyph and monkeys wore goggles fitted with Kodak Wratten filters (red #29 and green #61) to view the stimulus. This additionally provided binocular parallax.

claim: The binocular crosstalk for the green channel was 1.7%
source: The binocular crosstalk for the green and red channels was 1.7% and 2.3%, respectively.

claim: The binocular crosstalk for the red channel was 2.3%
source: The binocular crosstalk for the green and red channels was 1.7% and 2.3%, respectively.

claim: All behavioral data were recorded at a sampling rate of 833.33 Hz
source: All behavioral data were recorded along with the neural event markers at a sampling rate of 833.33 Hz.

claim: Monkeys received a drop of juice if their stopping position was within 0.6 m from the center of the target
source: They received a drop of juice if their stopping position was within 0.6 m from the center of the target.

claim: Broadband signals were amplified and digitized at 20 kHz using a multichannel data acquisition system for acute recordings
source: The broadband signals were amplified and digitized at 20 kHz using a multichannel data acquisition system (Plexon Inc, Dallas, TX, USA) and were stored along with the action potential waveforms for offline analysis.

claim: LFP signals were low-pass filtered at –3 dB at 250 Hz for acute recordings
source: Additionally, for each channel, we also stored low-pass filtered (–3 dB at 250 Hz) LFP signals.

claim: For chronic array recordings, broadband neural signals were amplified and digitized at 30 kHz
source: For the chronic array recordings, broadband neural signals were amplified and digitized at 30 kHz using a digital headstage (Cereplex E, Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT, USA)

claim: For chronic array recordings, LFP signals were low-pass filtered at –6 dB at 250 Hz and sampled at 500 Hz
source: Additionally, for each channel, we also stored low-pass filtered (–6 dB at 250 Hz) LFP signals sampled at 500 Hz.

claim: Spike detection and sorting were performed using KiloSort 2.0 software
source: Spike detection and sorting were performed on the raw (broadband) neural signals using KiloSort 2.0 software (Pachitariu et al., 2016) on an NVIDIA Quadro P5000 GPU.
evidence: Description of data analysis methods with citation

claim: Units were qualified as single units if ISIv <20%, cR <0.02, and PR >90%
source: We set the following thresholds in qualifying a unit as a single unit: ISIv <20%, cR <0.02, and PR >90%.

claim: A linear model with multiplicative gain accounted well for the observed data with average R²=0.72
source: As we have observed before (Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018; Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2020; Noel et al., 2020; Noel et al., 2021), a linear model with multiplicative gain accounted well for the observed data (average R2=0.72).
evidence: Model fit quality with citations to prior work

claim: Spike counts were sampled at a 6 ms resolution for the P-GAM
source: As such, inputs to the P-GAM were of three types. First, the spike counts of the unit to be modeled, at a 6 ms resolution (i.e., the number of spikes within 6 ms windows, no baseline correction).
evidence: Description of data processing for modeling

claim: The P-GAM used 15 knots per covariate defining the nodes of tuning functions
source: The last input type were a set of 15 'knots' per covariate, defining the nodes of eventual tuning functions.

claim: Knots were defined to cover the range from the 2nd to the 98th percentile with equi-probable spacing
source: The location of knots were defined as to (i) cover the range of a given input variable from the 2nd to the 98th percentile with (ii) equi-probable knots (each knot covering the same probability mass).

claim: Pseudo-R² is a goodness of fit measure suitable for models with Poisson observation noise
source: Pseudo-R2 is a goodness of fit measure that is suitable for models with Poisson observation noise (Colin Cameron and Windmeijer, 1997).
evidence: Description of statistical measure with citation

claim: The pseudo-R² score is 0 when the GAM fits are no more likely than the null model and 1 when it perfectly matches the data
source: The score is 0 when the GAM fits are no more likely than the null model, 1 when it perfectly matches the data, and rarely can be negative (for test-set data, 3% of the recorded units) when overfitting occurs.

claim: 3% of recorded units had negative pseudo-R² values indicating overfitting
source: The score is 0 when the GAM fits are no more likely than the null model, 1 when it perfectly matches the data, and rarely can be negative (for test-set data, 3% of the recorded units) when overfitting occurs. In this latter case we excluded the unit from analysis.
evidence: Quality control criterion for data analysis

claim: The average pseudo-R² score of 0.072 is about three times better than standard GLM performance in primary somatosensory and motor areas
source: Our average score of 0.072 is about three times better than standard GLM performance even in areas such as primary somatosensory and motor areas (Benjamin et al., 2018).

claim: The discrimination index was computed using 15 bins for linear and angular velocities
source: In the context of the current naturalistic experiment, we may bin linear and angular velocities and compute tuning functions defining Rmax and Rmin. The number of bins (here, we used 15 nodes, as defined by the P-GAM) defines M.

claim: Recordings were divided into 80 segments to match the mean number of trials in Chen et al., 2008
source: To facilitate direct comparison with Chen et al., 2008, we divided our recordings in 80 segments, the mean number of trials (N) in Chen et al., 2008.
evidence: Description of analysis method for comparison with prior work

claim: Spectral clustering was performed based on the Jaccard distance metric
source: For Figure 4A and B, clustering was performed by employing a spectral clustering algorithm based on the Jaccard distance metric (Shi and Malik, 2000).
evidence: Description of analysis method with citation

claim: The input matrix for clustering was 4254 neurons × 17 task variables
source: The results reported in the main text were generated for the full dataset, and thus a 4254 (231 MSTd neuron + 3200 7a neurons + 823 dlPFC neurons) × 17 (task variables) input matrix (where each entry denotes whether a particular neuron was significant or not for a particular task variable).
evidence: Description of data structure for analysis

claim: DBSCAN automatically determined the number of clusters based on the spatial density of the UMAPs
source: This clustering method automatically determined the number of clusters on the basis of the spatial density of the UMAPs.

claim: Within area coupling filters were set to a duration of 36 ms
source: Coupling filters (and the corresponding inferential statistics) were determined via the P-GAM. Within area coupling filters were set to a duration of 36 ms, and across area filters were set to a duration of 600 ms.

claim: Across area coupling filters were set to a duration of 600 ms
source: Coupling filters (and the corresponding inferential statistics) were determined via the P-GAM. Within area coupling filters were set to a duration of 36 ms, and across area filters were set to a duration of 600 ms.

claim: Within-area coupling probability was corrected for electrode distance by fitting a brain region-specific logistic regression
source: For the within-area coupling probability reported in Figure 4E, we corrected for the effects of unit distance (i.e., Figure 4—figure supplement 3A) by first fitting a brain region-specific logistic regression.

claim: The coupling probability in Figure 4E was set as the model prediction for a distance of 500 µm
source: Each brain area was fit independently, and the coupling probability in Figure 4E was set as the model prediction for a distance of 500 µm.

claim: UMAP conserves global structure and allows for meaningful interpretation of distances
source: Notably, however, the centroid of MSTd was 6.49 times closer to the centroid of dlPFC than area 7a (Figure 4C, top row. Note that Becht et al., 2018, have shown UMAP to conserve global structure and thus allows for a meaningful interpretation of distances).

claim: The centroid of MSTd was 6.49 times closer to the centroid of dlPFC than area 7a in UMAP space
source: Notably, however, the centroid of MSTd was 6.49 times closer to the centroid of dlPFC than area 7a (Figure 4C, top row. Note that Becht et al., 2018, have shown UMAP to conserve global structure and thus allows for a meaningful interpretation of distances).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of UMAP projections shown in Figure 4C

claim: When subsampling to match MSTd neuron count, MSTd-dlPFC distance was 5.56 times closer than MSTd-7a (95% CI = [4.07, 7.33])
source: This finding also holds when subsampling from 7a and dlPFC to match the number of units present in MSTd (100 iterations, MSTd-dlPFC distance was 5.56 times closer than MSTd-7a, 95% CI = [4.07, 7.33]; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis with subsampling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Cluster 1 in UMAP space contained 81.5% of all dlPFC neurons, 58.9% of all MSTd neurons, and 3.6% of all neurons from 7a
source: Cluster 1 (Figure 4C, second row) contained 81.5% of all dlPFC neurons, 58.9% of all MSTd neurons, and 3.6% of all neurons from 7a.
evidence: Quantitative clustering results shown in Figure 4C

claim: Clusters 2 and 3 in UMAP space exclusively contained neurons from area 7a
source: Clusters 2 and 3 exclusively contained neurons from area 7a (Figure 4C, third and fourth row).
